Jon - share KV cache benchmark spreadsheet and raw logs
Schedule on-prem pilot for week of 2025-09-01 (ArgoHealth to confirm nodes and network)

summary: Deep dive between Redwood AE/SE and ArgoHealth platform/security on Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs. Focus on runtime perf (latency/throughput), KV cache behavior, batching, quantization strategies, and VPC/on-prem connectivity. Customer interested in isolation guarantees and noisy-neighbor mitigation for a clinical workloads pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Morning everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood. We'll do a deep dive on dedicated vs hosted for the performance questions you sent over. Jon, our SE, will walk through benchmarks and some implementation details.
[00:12] Jon (SE): hey all, hi, quick intro — I'm Jon Ruiz, infra SE. I'll try to keep the kernel level bits high level but happy to dig in.
[00:22] Lena (CTO): hi Maya, Jon, thanks. We're trying to understand where we should start — hosted for speed or go straight to dedicated for isolation and throughput guarantees.
[00:32] Diego (Platform Eng): also need details on KV cache behavior. We're doing real-time clinical summarization, latency matters. p95 is a hard ask.
[00:40] Priya (Security): and from security side we need KMS/HSM notes and SOC2 evidence, and also on-prem options.
[00:49] Jon (SE): great, quick agenda: 1) runtime perf and typical latencies on hosted vs dedicated, 2) KV cache semantics and warm-up, 3) batching & continuous batching, 4) quantization options and impact on quality, 5) VPC/on-prem considerations and isolation, 6) Q&A and next steps.
[01:05] Maya (AE): perfect. Quick callouts — ArgoHealth mentioned 10k qps spikes and many short requests (20-50 tokens). We'll keep that pattern in mind.
[01:15] Jose (ML Eng): yes most calls are single-turn summarizations of 30 tokens output and 80 token context, so throughput per GPU matters.
[01:25] Jon (SE): ok first, latency baseline. On Redwood Hosted with our multitenant pools for an Llama-2-like 70B variant on H100, typical p50/p95 for 32 token generations looks like ~80ms / ~220ms when there's no heavy contention; but you should expect variability due to noisy neighbors on shared pools.
[01:44] Jon (SE): on Dedicated with reserved A100/H100 pools, we hit ~70ms p50 and p95 closer to 120-140ms for same payload, because you reduce queueing and get predictable kernel selection. The exact numbers depend on batch size and sequence length distribution.
[02:05] Diego: so dedicated buys us more consistent p95 — what about throughput?
[02:11] Jon: dedicated can be right-sized — e.g., a single H100 node can sustain X tokens/s for your workload, and with reserved capacity we give a throughput guarantee based on committed nodes and autoscale policy. On hosted you get burst but not strong throughput SLOs.
[02:26] Maya: note that our Hosted offering has soft throttles and capacity pools that can burst but we don't give the same contractual throughput guarantee as Dedicated.
[02:35] Priya: what about noisy neighbor / isolation specifics? If a tenant co-located on same GPU does heavy batching, could that spike our p95?
[02:44] Jon: yes, in multitenant pools there is potential for interference. We mitigate with dynamic scheduling, cgroups, and per-request QoS heuristics but it's not perfect. Dedicated gives CPU/GPU isolation at the VM and node level so noisy neighbor risk is essentially eliminated. Also we can do NUMA pinning and tune kernel launches on Dedicated.
[03:05] Lena: any examples of noisy neighbor causing visible degradation?
[03:09] Jon: we had a case where a large batching job (long sequence gen) overloaded a shared worker and increased p95 by ~40% for others for a 10 minute window. We have fallback routing after detection, but paid Dedicated avoids that class of issues.
[03:25] [00:03:25] Speaker 2 (Customer): okay makes sense.
[03:30] Jon: moving to KV cache — our runtime uses an LRU-style KV caching of KV tensors per model shard. For single-turn summarization you get big wins because prefix isn't long, but for multi-turn chat KV cache is crucial.
[03:46] Jon: cache warm-up: first requests populate the KV cache and you can see an initial latency hit; after warming p95 drops significantly. Dedicated helps because cache residency is more stable — on hosted we may evict keys under heavy churn.
[03:58] Diego: how often are keys evicted on hosted? We have thousands of concurrent users, each with short-lived sessions.
[04:06] Jon: eviction depends on pool pressure; in synthetic tests with high churn we saw eviction rates that caused a ~25% throughput loss vs steady state. We can provide your expected session profile into our simulator and estimate eviction.
[04:20] Lena: can we pin user sessions to nodes?
[04:23] Jon: on Dedicated yes, you can pin routing by customer or route; on Hosted we do sticky routing heuristics but not strict node pinning.
[04:31] Priya: is KV cache encrypted at rest / in transit?
[04:35] Jon: KV tensors are stored in memory on the node; for Dedicated and Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and disk encryption. On Hosted, in-memory caches are transient and we use encryption in transit; persistent checkpoints use KMS. We'll share the security docs.
[04:49] Maya: note for Private/on-prem we also support HSM integrations if you require that.
[04:55] Jose: batching — you mentioned continuous batching. How deterministic is it for low-latency small requests?
[05:02] Jon: continuous batching groups small requests into kernel-sized batches up to a configurable latency cap; for small single-turn 30 token outputs we typically configure a 10-25ms max batch delay. That gives better GPU utilization while keeping p95 acceptable. But if you set batch delay to 0 you get no batching and poor GPU utilization.
[05:21] Diego: what's the perf delta for batching vs no batching?
[05:24] Jon: for your workload we saw batching improve tokens/sec per GPU by 2.5-3x at 10-25ms batching window, while p50 stays similar and p95 increases modestly (depending on traffic shape). On Dedicated you can tune that window more aggressively.
[05:40] Maya: also remember prefix/KV cache reduces the need for repeated compute so batching + cache together give multiplicative improvements.
[05:48] Lena: quantization — we need to keep clinical accuracy, any quality regressions with int8/int4?
[05:55] Jon: quantization profiles vary by model. Our Platform supports int8 and mixed int8/4 workflows; we recommend starting with int8 quantization profiles we validated (Redwood-verified profiles). For sensitive clinical tasks, we recommend evals on your prompts — we can run A/B between fp16 and int8 to measure delta. Typical delta is small but could matter depending on hallucination tolerance.
[06:14] Jose: do you support quantization-aware kernels on H100 vs A100?
[06:18] Jon: yes kernels are hardware-aware — H100 has better int8 throughput on some ops, and our compilation step chooses kernels. On Dedicated you can pick instance type; on Hosted we route to pools with variant hardware.
[06:31] Diego: regressions: how do you surface quality drops after quantization or model changes?
[06:35] Jon: Redwood Optimize ties eval suites to production routes; we can set regression alerts on metrics like token-likelihood delta, embedding drift, and custom rubric scores. If a rollout causes regressions we trigger automatic rollback.
[06:50] Priya: networking for VPC/private — how does traffic path look for Private vs Dedicated in our VPC?
[06:56] Jon: Dedicated offers VPC peering and private link; data plane can be inside your VPC for Dedicated-private deployments. For Private/on-prem we deploy control plane separate from data plane; data never leaves your network if you choose air-gapped. We'll share the network diagrams.
[07:12] Lena: latency implications of VPC peering?
[07:15] Jon: peering adds minimal latency (~1-5ms) depending on region and network. Biggest contributors remain model inference and batching. For tight p95 SLAs we recommend colocating inference nodes in the same region/AZ as the app tier.
[07:29] Diego: throughput guarantees — how do you calc them? We need contractual numbers for SREs.
[07:34] Jon: we size committed nodes based on your expected qps and model selection; throughput guarantees in Dedicated are expressed as tokens/sec per committed node with autoscale buffers. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet — that's the burst policy matrix Maya mentioned.
[07:47] Maya: I'll attach the matrix and an example SLO calculation for a 10k qps pattern.
[07:52] Lena: can we do a short pilot to validate numbers? Ideally on-prem or VPC/private.
[07:57] Maya: yes, pilot works — we usually do a 2-week pilot with telemetry and a benchmark harness. On-prem pilot requires some infra readiness checklist.
[08:07] Jose: for the pilot can we run our test prompts and measure p50/p95 and throughput?
[08:12] Jon: absolutely — we can run your prompt set and return the same metrics, plus KV cache warm-up curves. We also capture trace-level logs to see time spent in kernel vs memory copy vs network.
[08:25] [00:08:25] Speaker 1 (Customer): how do you handle model fallbacks if a Dedicated node fails?
[08:30] Jon: Dedicated clusters have redundancy and autoscale policies; we also provide configured fallback to a hosted pool for availability, though that changes your isolation guarantees. You can define failover policies per route.
[08:44] Priya: on regulatory stuff, what's in the SOC2 pack?
[08:47] Maya: we'll share SOC2 Type II report, data retention policies, access control docs, KMS integration guides and audit log formats. Priya we can set a follow-up session specifically for security deep dive.
[08:58] Priya: yes please.
[09:02] Diego: are there specific kernel optimizations you do for KV cache? I saw mention of fused attention and KV cache packing in your docs.
[09:08] Jon: yes we use fused attention kernels and pack KV tensors to improve memory locality. On Dedicated we can tune memory placement to keep KV cache in GPU or pinned host memory depending on model size. That reduces PCIe transfers.
[09:22] Jose: for models that exceed single-GPU mem, do you recommend sharded KV across GPUs or model parallel?
[09:28] Jon: we support tensor/model sharding; sharded KV across GPUs is standard and we expose config for shard placement. For low-latency you want minimal cross-GPU comms; Dedicated lets you pick larger-memory nodes to avoid sharding.
[09:43] Lena: what's the cost delta roughly between Hosted and Dedicated for our profile? ballpark.
[09:48] Maya: Hosted is lower upfront; Dedicated is higher committed but reduces per-token cost at scale. We'll send a tailored pricing example — generally at sustained loads of X tokens/sec you break even within months depending on model.
[09:59] Jon: also consider operational overhead — Dedicated reduces surprises from noisy neighbors and gives you stronger SLAs.
[10:06] Diego: any gotchas for on-prem? firewall, GPUs drivers, kernel compat?
[10:10] Jon: on-prem requires hardware validation: drivers, CUDA versions, GPU firmware and network MTU tuning. We provide a checklist and a small validation suite. Also for air-gapped, we do encrypted artifact transfer and local package registry.
[10:25] Priya: how do you handle logging and audit trail? We need immutable logs for compliance.
[10:30] Maya: Dedicated/Private provide audit logs streaming to your SIEM; we support integrations (Splunk, Datadog) and signed logs for immutability.
[10:40] Diego: what about token accounting per customer when we route through Dedicated?
[10:44] Jon: billing-level token accounting is per-route and per-customer. We emit detailed usage rows and cost breakdown (kernel time, cache hit rate, tokens).
[10:54] Lena: we need a concretes list of metrics for SREs — p50/p95, tokens/sec per node, KV hit rate, evictions, queued requests, kernel time.
[11:04] Jon: yep we'll include that in the shared benchmarking doc.
[11:02] Maya: okay quick recap before open Qs — Dedicated = better isolation, predictable p95, throughput guarantees and advanced tuning (NUMA pinning, kernel selection). Hosted = faster start, lower upfront cost, flexible burst but less strong SLAs and some noisy-neighbor risk. KV cache and batching interplay is huge for cost/latency. Quantization can reduce cost but needs evals. VPC/private covers compliance and can be air-gapped.
[11:25] Diego: one more — can we have dedicated nodes but shared model variants to reduce cost? like shared model weights but dedicated execution?
[11:32] Jon: you can use model variants; one pattern is shared model storage with dedicated execution pools — reduces storage replication but execution isolation remains. We'll detail tradeoffs.
[11:45] Jose: any known limitations for Llama-3 style models?
[11:49] Jon: large models mainly impact memory and KV sizes; our kernel selection supports up to XB models and we recommend Dedicated for the largest models to avoid cross-tenant memory pressure.
[11:59] Maya: ok if there are no big blockers let's confirm next steps — I'll send pricing and matrix, Jon will share the KV benchmarks and a draft pilot plan. Priya we'll schedule security deep dive.
[12:10] Lena: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:13] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up by Thursday. Links referenced: Redwood benchmarks: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/dedicated-vs-hosted (internal), KV cache sim spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/internal/kvbench (shared drive).
[12:30] [END]
